title: Niépce and the View from the Window
summary: A patient French inventor named Niépce coated a metal plate with sticky black tar and pointed his camera out of an upstairs window. The sun shone on it for hours, maybe even days. When he washed the plate, a ghostly view of rooftops and trees appeared, and it is still the oldest camera photograph in the world.

sections.heading: A Gentleman Tinkerer in Burgundy
paragraphs: Imagine a big stone country house in Burgundy, in eastern France, surrounded by fields, barns and a courtyard with a pear tree. The house is called Le Gras, and it stands near the little village of Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, a few kilometres outside the town of Chalon-sur-Saône. In the 1820s, an upstairs room of this house was not a bedroom or a library. It was a workshop full of bottles, metal plates, lenses and wooden boxes, and it belonged to a man who could not stop experimenting.

His name was Joseph Nicéphore Niépce (say it 'nee-EPS'). He was born in Chalon-sur-Saône on 7 March 1765, the son of a wealthy lawyer. He had been a student, a soldier and a local official during the stormy years of the French Revolution and the wars that followed. Around 1801 he and his older brother Claude came home to the family estates and became what people then called gentlemen-farmers. They grew beets, helped make sugar, and spent a great deal of their time and money on inventions.

The two brothers dreamed big. As you saw in the last part, they built the Pyréolophore, one of the earliest internal combustion engines, which pushed a boat along a river by burning fuel in little puffs. They also experimented with ways to make dyes and with other machines. Claude eventually moved to England to try to sell their engine there, while Nicéphore stayed in Burgundy and turned more and more of his attention to a different puzzle: how to make pictures with light.

Part of his interest came from a craze sweeping France at the time called lithography, a new way of printing pictures from a flat slab of limestone. Artists drew on the stone with greasy crayon, then the stone was wetted and inked so that the ink stuck only to the greasy lines. Niépce loved the idea of printing pictures, but he was not a skilled artist. If only, he thought, light itself could draw the picture onto the plate for him.

By about 1816 he was already pointing small camera obscuras out of his windows. He called these views 'points de vue', which means 'points of view'. With paper soaked in silver chloride he managed to catch faint images, but they came out as negatives, with light and dark reversed, and he could not stop them from darkening further in daylight. Like Wedgwood and Davy before him, he had run straight into the fixing problem. So he went looking for a completely different kind of light-sensitive material.

sections.heading: Sun Writing with Sticky Tar
paragraphs: The material Niépce settled on sounds like something from a road crew, not an art studio. It was bitumen of Judea, a natural asphalt: a thick, dark, tar-like substance that seeps out of the ground in a few places in the world, including around the Dead Sea. (Judea was the old name for part of that region, which is how the bitumen got its name.) People had used it for thousands of years to waterproof boats and baskets. Printmakers in Niépce's time also used it, because acid could not eat through it, which made it useful for etching designs into metal.

Bitumen has a strange and wonderful property. When it sits in bright light for a long time, it slowly hardens. Chemists today explain that the light causes its long molecules to link together into a tougher network. Hardened bitumen no longer dissolves easily in certain oils. Bitumen that has stayed in the dark, on the other hand, still dissolves.

That was all Niépce needed. Here is his recipe, step by step. First, he dissolved powdered bitumen in oil of lavender, the same sweet-smelling oil used in perfumes. Second, he spread a very thin coat of this mixture over a carefully polished plate and let it dry. Third, he put the plate into a camera and pointed it at a scene, or he laid a printed picture right on top of the plate and set it in the sun. Fourth, after a long time in the light, he washed the plate with a mixture of lavender oil and white petroleum (a light, clear oil). Wherever light had struck strongly, the hardened bitumen stayed stuck to the plate. Wherever it had been dark, the soft bitumen washed away, leaving bare metal.

The result was a picture made of two things side by side: pale patches of hardened bitumen and darker patches of shiny bare metal. Because the bright parts of the scene became the pale bitumen, the image was a positive, not a negative, when viewed at the right angle. Niépce named his process héliographie, or heliography, from the Greek words 'helios' (sun) and 'graphein' (to write or draw). Heliography means 'sun writing'.

Niépce tried his bitumen on all sorts of surfaces: glass, copper, silver-coated copper, zinc, pewter and even limestone. On glass, he could look through the picture as if it were a window. On metal, he hoped that the bitumen could act as a mask for acid, so that the bare areas could be etched into grooves, inked and printed again and again like an engraving. In other words, he wasn't only trying to make a single picture. He was trying to invent a printing machine powered by the sun.

sections.heading: Copying Pictures Without an Artist
paragraphs: Before Niépce tackled the harder task of photographing the real world, he practised on something easier: copying existing pictures. Engravings were printed on fairly thin paper. If he soaked an engraving in oil, the paper became partly see-through. He could then lay it directly on a bitumen-coated plate, black lines down, and leave it in the sun. Light passed through the blank paper and hardened the bitumen beneath, but the black lines blocked the light, so the bitumen under them stayed soft and washed away. This method, with the original pressed right against the plate and no lens at all, is called contact printing.

In 1822 Niépce made what he and many historians regard as the first permanent image made by light: a heliographic copy of an engraved portrait of Pope Pius VII on glass. Sadly, it no longer exists. He later tried to make printed copies from it, and the plate was destroyed in the process. For an inventor this was the normal price of progress: the best evidence was often used up by the next experiment.

Others survive. From around 1825 there are heliographs of old engravings, including one showing a man leading a horse. A famous one from 1826 copies an engraving of Cardinal Georges d'Amboise, a French churchman of the 1500s. From about 1825 Niépce worked with a Paris engraver named Augustin François Lemaître, who helped etch plates and made ink prints on paper from them, showing that sun-made images could indeed be turned into printing plates.

Altogether, a small number of Niépce's heliographic plates and prints from the later 1820s survive in museums and libraries today. They look faint and brownish, a bit like old pencil rubbings. But they prove something astonishing. For the first time in history, a picture had been copied by light and chemistry alone, without a human hand drawing a single line.

There was a big difference, though, between copying an engraving and capturing the world outside. An engraving pressed against a plate in full sunshine sends a lot of light onto the bitumen. A camera obscura, by contrast, gathers only a little light from a scene and spreads it over the plate as a dim image. Bitumen was very slow to react even in direct sun. Making it record a dim camera image would test Niépce's patience like nothing before.

sections.heading: The View from the Upstairs Window
paragraphs: Sometime around 1826 or 1827, probably in the summer of 1827, Niépce climbed to his upstairs workroom at Le Gras and set up a camera obscura beside an open window. Inside the camera he placed a polished sheet of pewter, a grey metal made mostly of tin mixed with a little lead, coated with his thin layer of bitumen. The plate measured about 16.2 by 20.2 centimetres, roughly the size of a small notebook. Then he pointed the lens out at the view he saw every day: the rooftops and walls of the farm buildings around his courtyard, with trees and open sky beyond.

Then he waited. And waited. Nobody living today knows exactly how long that plate sat in the camera, but it was certainly many hours, and quite possibly several days. When Niépce finally took it out and washed it with his lavender oil and white petroleum, a picture remained. It was blurry, grainy and strange, but it was there: on the left, part of the upstairs of the house; a tall pigeon house or loft; a slanting barn roof in the middle; the tops of trees; and on the right, another wing of the building. It was the world outside his window, drawn by the sun itself.

Today this plate is known as View from the Window at Le Gras, and it is the oldest surviving photograph taken with a camera. Niépce had very likely made earlier camera views, and he had made heliographic copies of engravings before it, but every older camera image has been lost. This one, by a mixture of luck and care, is still with us almost two hundred years later.

If you look at a good reproduction, you might at first see only a jumble of grey shapes, a bit like looking at clouds. The trick is to find the roofline. Once your eye spots the triangle of the barn roof in the middle, the rest of the scene snaps into place, and you are suddenly standing in a French farmhouse two centuries ago, looking out of the same window as Niépce.

The real plate is even harder to see than the copies. It is a mirror-like sheet of metal with a very thin, pale layer on top, so the picture only appears when light hits it at just the right angle. Tilt it a little and it vanishes into a shiny blank. Niépce himself was modest about his results, treating them as only a first, uncertain step in a completely new direction. He was right on both counts: the step was uncertain, and the direction was completely new.

sections.heading: Sunshine on Both Sides
paragraphs: How long did the exposure really take? For many years, books gave a neat answer: about eight hours. That number came from a clever clue inside the picture itself. Look closely and the buildings seem to be lit by the sun on both their left and right sides at once. In real life, of course, the sun moves across the sky from east to west during the day. In the morning it lights one side of a building; by afternoon it lights the other. A picture showing sunshine on both sides must have been exposed through much of a day, while the sun swung across the sky.

More recent research suggests that eight hours may have been far too short. Researchers who carefully recreated Niépce's bitumen process, using his materials and methods, found that a camera image like this probably needed several days of light to form. If that is right, the plate may have sat in the camera through many sunrises and sunsets, catching the sun from many angles. This is why careful historians now say the exposure lasted 'hours, possibly days', rather than giving one exact number.

Either way, the long exposure explains why there are no people, animals or carts in the picture. Anything that moved simply did not stay in one place long enough to leave a mark. A cat strolling across the courtyard, a farm worker pushing a wheelbarrow, birds landing on the roof: all of them would have been far too quick. Only the buildings, which did not move for days, were recorded. For a photograph of the real world to include people, the exposure time would have to shrink from hours to minutes, and that would take another inventor and another chemistry.

It is worth pausing to imagine how this felt. Niépce had no light meter, no instructions and no one to ask. Every experiment meant coating a plate, waiting a long time, washing it and hoping. Most attempts failed. Some plates showed nothing at all; others came out as a fog. He worked like this for years, writing long letters to his brother Claude in England about every small success and setback. The View from the Window is not the result of one lucky afternoon. It is the reward for about ten years of stubborn trial and error.

sections.heading: A Disappointing Trip to England
paragraphs: In 1827, Niépce received worrying news: his brother Claude was seriously ill in England. Claude had been living near London for years, trying to find investors for their engine and spending much of the family fortune in the process. Nicéphore and his wife Agnès set out to visit him. On the way, they stopped in Paris, and there Niépce met a famous showman and painter named Louis Daguerre, who had heard about his experiments and was eager to talk. Keep that name in mind; it will matter a great deal.

When Niépce reached England in September 1827, he found Claude in poor health and, sadly, not entirely clear in his mind. Claude's grand hopes for the engine had come to nothing. While staying near London, Niépce met Francis Bauer, a talented botanical artist who painted plants for the royal gardens at Kew. Bauer looked at the heliographs Niépce had brought, including the View from the Window, and was impressed. He encouraged Niépce to present his discovery to the Royal Society of London, the most famous scientific society in Britain.

Niépce wrote a short paper, which he called a notice on heliography, and offered it to the Society. But there was a snag. Niépce did not want to explain his full method. He hoped one day to earn money from it, and he feared that if he gave away every detail, someone else would profit instead. The Royal Society had a rule against considering secret processes: if you wanted scientists to take your discovery seriously, you had to tell them how it worked so they could test it. Because Niépce kept the key steps to himself, the Society would not consider his paper.

Disappointed, Niépce returned to France in early 1828. Before he left, he gave his paper and several of his heliographs, including the View from the Window, to Francis Bauer. Claude died in England in 1828, destitute after spending so much on the brothers' inventions. It was a sad journey in every way. Yet by leaving his plates with Bauer, Niépce accidentally did something enormously important: he made sure that his oldest camera image would be kept safe in England, far from the experiments in his workshop that destroyed so many of his other pictures.

sections.heading: Two Inventors Join Forces
paragraphs: Back at Le Gras, Niépce knew his bitumen process had a serious weakness: it was simply too slow. A picture that needed hours or days of sunshine could never capture people, animals or busy streets. He needed better lenses, more sensitive materials, and money. Daguerre, the showman he had met in Paris, was well connected and full of energy, and he was also experimenting with light-sensitive chemicals. Daguerre had reportedly learned about Niépce through the Chevalier family, well-known Paris opticians who sold lenses to both men.

In December 1829 the two men signed a formal partnership agreement. Niépce, as the inventor of heliography, would share his secret process. Daguerre would contribute his own ideas, skill and energy, and help improve the method and make it known. Any profits would be shared. For the next few years, they wrote to each other regularly, reportedly sometimes using code numbers instead of chemical names so that nosy postal clerks or rivals could not steal their ideas.

Together they tried many new materials. One process they developed, around 1832, used the sticky residue left after distilling lavender oil, dissolved in alcohol, as the light-sensitive layer. They called it the physautotype. Like the later daguerreotype, a physautotype was a one-of-a-kind picture that looked positive or negative depending on how the light reflected off it. It was faster than the old bitumen method, but still far too slow for portraits.

Meanwhile both men also experimented with silver-coated plates. Letters between the partners from about 1831 and 1832 show that Daguerre was especially interested in polished silver treated with iodine fumes, which formed a thin light-sensitive layer. This would turn out to be the winning path, but neither man knew it yet.

sections.heading: Lost, Found and Kept Safe in Texas
paragraphs: On 5 July 1833, Nicéphore Niépce suffered a stroke at Le Gras and died, aged 68. He had spent so much of the family fortune on inventions that he died nearly penniless. The local town council paid for his grave in the little cemetery of Saint-Loup-de-Varennes, close to the house where he had made his sun pictures. He was buried without knowing that, just six years later, photography would be announced to the world and celebrated in newspapers across Europe and America. His son, Isidore Niépce, took his father's place in the partnership with Daguerre.

And what happened to the View from the Window? After Francis Bauer died in 1840, Niépce's plates were sold and passed from one British owner to another. In 1839, while Bauer was still alive, they had been shown at the Royal Society, as the excitement about new photographic inventions grew. After that, the oldest camera photograph in the world slowly faded from memory. By the early 1900s it had been put away, and for decades almost nobody knew where it was.

Then, in 1952, two photography historians, Helmut Gernsheim and his wife Alison, tracked it down after a long search. Helmut was a German-born photographer and collector living in Britain, and he was building one of the greatest collections of early photographs ever assembled. When he finally held the pewter plate, he realised he was looking at the beginning of photography itself.

Showing it to the world was harder than finding it. The image was so faint that ordinary photographs of it came out as a confusing grey smear. The Gernsheims asked an expert at the Kodak Research Laboratory in England to make a copy, and it took great effort to capture even part of what the eye could see on the plate. Helmut then retouched one copy heavily by hand, painting in details to make the scene clearer. For many years, until the late 1970s, that retouched version was the only one he allowed to be published, so many older books show a picture that is part Niépce and part Gernsheim.

In 1963, the University of Texas at Austin bought most of the Gernsheim Collection, thanks to Harry Ransom, a university leader who wanted to build a world-class library and research centre. Niépce's plate travelled across the Atlantic with thousands of other early photographs. Today it is kept at the Harry Ransom Center in Austin, where it is normally on display in the main lobby.

Looking after it is serious science. Between 2002 and 2003, experts from the Getty Conservation Institute in California studied the plate closely. They confirmed that the image really is made of bitumen and that the plate is pewter: mostly tin with lead, plus tiny traces of iron, copper and nickel. They also noticed small bumps that had formed near three of its corners, which catch the light and make the picture even harder to see. To protect it, the Getty team designed a special sealed display case filled with an inert gas instead of air, so there is no oxygen to slowly corrode the metal. Sensors keep watch on the conditions inside all the time.

So if you ever visit Austin, you can stand in front of a small dark frame and see, very faintly, the same rooftops that Niépce saw from his window almost two hundred years ago. It is one of the most precious objects in the history of science, and it fits in a frame smaller than a school notebook.

Niépce never became famous in his lifetime, and for many years after his death his partner's name was far better known. Today, though, historians agree that the very first surviving photograph from a camera is his, and his home in Burgundy has become a place of pilgrimage for photographers. The town of Chalon-sur-Saône, where he was born, has a museum of photography named after him.

But the story did not stop at Le Gras. When Niépce died in 1833, his partner was left alone in Paris with a pile of letters, notes, recipes and half-finished experiments. Daguerre was not a patient country gentleman. He was a theatre man, used to dazzling crowds. Holding Niépce's notes in his workshop, he made up his mind: pictures that took hours were no use to anyone. He would find a way to make the sun draw in minutes.

deepDive: Why was Niépce's camera image so slow, and why do historians argue about its exposure time? Bitumen of Judea is a complex natural mixture of large carbon-based molecules. Light, especially ultraviolet and blue light, slowly causes these molecules to cross-link into a tougher, less soluble network. That is a direct chemical change: every bit of hardening must be caused by light energy actually arriving at that spot. There is no amplification. The daguerreotype and later silver processes, by contrast, depend on a latent image. A few photons create tiny specks of silver, and then a developer multiplies the effect enormously. That difference in chemistry explains why the bitumen process needed hours or days, while Daguerre's needed minutes. The traditional figure of about eight hours came from the observation that sunlight seems to strike both sides of the buildings. In the 1990s and 2000s, researchers who reconstructed the process, notably the French researcher Jean-Louis Marignier, concluded that a camera image of this kind would need several days. That would also explain the double lighting, since the sun would light each side many times over. Because nobody recorded the exposure, the honest answer is 'hours, possibly days'. The date is also debated: Gernsheim first dated the plate to 1826, while later study of Niépce's letters points to the summer of 1827. Another debate concerns credit. Niépce's 1822 contact copy of an engraving may have been the first permanent image made by light, but it was destroyed, so the Le Gras plate holds the title of oldest surviving camera photograph. Historians also note that the plate's visibility depends heavily on lighting: the image consists of thin bitumen on reflective metal, so it can look positive, negative or invisible depending on viewing angle. Modern scientific study, including work by the Getty Conservation Institute and analysis by the Louvre's laboratory in 2007 using ion beams, has examined slow oxidation of the metal, which is why the plate now lives in an oxygen-free case. Finally, Niépce's secrecy shaped history. By refusing to publish his method in 1827, he lost the chance for early recognition, and the public announcement of photography in 1839 came under Daguerre's name instead.
funFact: Niépce's printing plates were coated with the same kind of natural asphalt that ancient peoples used to waterproof boats, and he dissolved it in lavender oil, so his workshop probably smelled like a perfume shop mixed with a road crew.
